prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Like nights we knelt on the dirt floor of a dugout, leaned our heads back, eyes twitching gone, and popped nitrous canisters into the communion shapes of our mouths, slipped inside where everything seemed to be falling snow, ice, the time split between chasing flies through a darkened park and sprawling in sycamore bark—how clean that abyss we drifted in, like dew, more like pollen, on our skins; and, beneath, a want for touch, a kiss, a return. Like nothing back then, to break an arm latching on to the bumper of an Impala, or settling back as the car took us as far as the salted bridge, before letting the ride go with a mitten caught behind the chrome waving from the other side of the river. Like this, you said, sliding a needle, watching dope plunge, the body's rush and tow until you felt something like an angel hovering above, but it was only pigeon feathers deviling the air. Those friends are gone: some dead, dying, locked up or jailed in themselves; and when I see some kids running in the heat of a taillight swirling behind them, I remember we wanted only to quiet our bodies, their unnatural hum, a vague pull inward, some thin furrows gliding over the snow.

I recall evening after evening spent on our knees against the earth floor of a baseball shelter. We would tilt our faces skyward, our gaze rolling back in delirium, as we discharged laughing gas into our reverent, gaping mouths. We drifted into a mental state that felt like frozen winter precipitation, during a period divided between chasing insects through pitch-black parks and resting our bodies against the rough bark of sycamore trees. The void through which we floated felt remarkably pure, settling on our skin like a fine dust of spores or early morning condensation. Yet beneath that euphoric haze lay a deep craving for intimacy, physical affection, and a way back home. 

In those years, suffering a fractured bone meant nothing to us when we hitched rides by clinging to the rear fender of a Chevy sedan. We slid along until reaching a salted bridge, finally releasing our grip and leaving a winter glove trapped on the vehicle’s metallic trim—looking like a hand waving goodbye from the opposite side of the water. 

"It feels like this," you remarked while depressing a syringe, watching the narcotic enter your vein, triggering a powerful physical tide. For a moment, you believed a heavenly spirit was hovering overhead, though it was actually just a swirl of loose pigeon plumage drifting in the breeze. 

Those companions from my youth are no longer around: some have passed away or are nearing death, while others are incarcerated or trapped within their own minds. Whenever I observe young people today sprinting through the red glow of swirling car lights, I remember our true motive: we simply sought to hush the restless vibration of our own flesh, to ease that subtle internal gravity, leaving behind only faint tracks gliding across the winter snow.
outputs.L3:
In my youth, my friends and I lived in the shadow of a desperate need to escape. We were constantly searching for a way out of the heavy reality we inhabited, turning to whatever could dull the world around us. Whether it was the brief, lightheaded euphoria of nitrous oxide or the suffocating, heavy warmth of heroin, we used these substances not merely to chase a high, but to systematically turn off the noise of our lives. 

Beneath our dangerous and reckless behavior lay a profound, unspoken hunger. We pushed boundaries, flirted with catastrophe, and placed ourselves in harm's way not out of true fearlessness, but out of a deep craving for connection. Every risky act was a tacit cry for physical touch, for validation, and for a sense of belonging. In our isolation, we forged a fragile brotherhood through shared danger, desperately clinging to one another to feel alive.

For fleeting moments, the drugs gave us exactly what we sought. The highs created a transcendent illusion, temporarily painting over the gray, harsh environment we called home. Suspended in those synthetic hazes, our pain felt distant, and the bleakness of our surroundings was briefly disguised by an artificial magic. But these moments were always borrowed time, leaving us exposed to an even colder reality when the chemicals inevitably wore off.

As the years passed, the bill for our lifestyle finally came due, and our tight-knit circle scattered to tragic fates. The heavy toll of our choices claimed many of us: some of my closest friends ended up in early graves, while others vanished behind the bars of prison cells. Even those who managed to survive physically remain emotionally trapped, frozen in time and forever haunted by the trauma of our youth. 

Today, whenever I see young people engaging in that same wild, unbridled recklessness, a profound sense of empathy washes over me. Looking at them, I am reminded of what truly drove us back then. Our past behavior was never just mindless rebellion; it was a desperate, chaotic effort to quiet a deep inner restlessness—a misguided search for warmth in a cold world, undertaken by kids who simply wanted to be held, seen, and understood.
outputs.L4:
The silence inside our heads was always too loud. 

We were nineteen, living in a decaying coastal town where the air tasted like salt and rust, carrying an unbearable weight we couldn't quite articulate. Julian carried the memory of a father who left and a mother who disappeared into bottle after bottle; Marcus was suffocating under the impossible expectations of a family that only saw his failures; and I was simply drowning in an invisible, paralyzing anxiety that made breathing feel like swallowing glass. We were drawn to one another not by common interests, but by a shared, desperate need to stop feeling so painfully alone in our pain.

At first, the remedy was simple: we chased the quiet. But normal outlets were useless against the magnitude of our inner noise. We needed remedies that hit harder, fast enough to outrun our thoughts.

It started with small dares, which quickly spiraled into terrifying rituals. We became adrenaline addicts, seeking solace in the razor’s edge between life and death. We would scale the rusted girders of the abandoned rail bridge at midnight, balanced precariously over the black, churning waters sixty feet below. We ran across the slippery roofs of downtown buildings, leaping three-story gaps with nothing but bravado and momentum keeping us from the concrete. 

To sharpen the high—and to dull the terrifying realization of what we were doing—we introduced substances. Cheap bourbon gave way to stolen prescription opioids, which eventually surrendered to whatever powder or pills Marcus could secure from the dark corners of the docks. Combined, the drugs and the stunts created a intoxicating cocktail. When you are suspended in mid-air, high on chemical euphoria, your past cannot touch you. Your trauma cannot find you. For a fleeting, shining second, the turmoil stopped, and we felt bound to one another by a sacred, invulnerable magic.

We thought we were invincible. We were just bleeding out in slow motion.

The illusion shattered on a humid Saturday night in August. We had gathered at the old grain silos on the edge of town—concrete monoliths rising a hundred feet into the dark sky. We were heavily intoxicated, floating on a dangerous concoction of synthetic narcotics and alcohol that Marcus had brought to celebrate the end of summer.

Julian, whose eyes had carried a vacant, desperate hollow all evening, decided he was going to leap the eight-foot gap between the twin silos. It was a jump he had made sober, but tonight, his balance was stolen by the toxins in his blood.

I remember screaming at him to stop, but the wind snatched my voice away. Marcus cheered him on, his judgment completely clouded by the pills. Julian took three staggered steps forward, smiled a heartbreaking, terrified smile, and launched himself into the dark.

He missed the ledge by inches.

The sound of his fall, and the absolute silence that followed, will haunt me until the day I die.

The aftermath was a slow-motion avalanche that swept away whatever was left of us. Julian died instantly on the cold gravel below. 

The police investigation was swift and unforgiving. When the toxicology reports revealed the lethal dose of narcotics in Julian’s system, the authorities looked for someone to blame. They found Marcus. Because he had procured and distributed the drugs that catalyzed the fatal night, he was prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. I watched from the gallery, numb, as Marcus—crying, frail, and stripped of all his posture—was sentenced to fifteen years in a maximum-security prison. His youth was erased with the slam of a gavel.

And then there was me. 

Physically, I walked away without a scratch. But spiritually, I was buried in that gravel alongside Julian. The guilt of not stopping him, the horror of that night, and the sudden, violent erasure of my only friends shattered my mind. I spent the next three years in and out of psychiatric facilities, haunted by nightmares, unable to hold a job, look people in the eye, or exist in a room without checking the ceiling for a way out. 

The peace we had so desperately sought through self-destruction turned out to be a cruel lie. We had set fire to ourselves just to keep warm, believing that the flames would weld us together and burn away our agony. Instead, the fire did what fire always does. It consumed Julian’s life, stole Marcus’s freedom, and left me standing in the ashes—living proof that trying to drown your demons only teaches them how to swim.
outputs.L5:
As the sun dipped below the horizon, painting the savanna in shades of burnt orange and deep amber, a quiet stillness settled over the open plain. Out in the distance, a herd moved with an effortless grace that seemed almost otherworldly. **Those** magnificent creatures, the **impala**, glided across the golden grass, their rust-colored coats catching the last rays of fading light. 

To watch them bound across the terrain was **like** witnessing poetry in motion—each leap was high, weightless, and briefly suspended in the cool evening air as if gravity had momentarily lost its hold. In moments such as this, the noise of the modern world faded away entirely, leaving only the rhythm of the wilderness and the silent, timeless beauty of the African twilight.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem exploring the reckless, self-destructive habits of youth, blending gritty details of drug use with lyrical nostalgia for lost friends.
counterfactuals.output:
We swallowed the moon in half-gram increments, leaning against damp alley brick that smelled of rain and rust. Remember how the streetlights haloed your head, Julian, like a saint constructed entirely out of low-grade speed and stale tobacco? We were holy then, or thought we were, our blood running hot with crushed blue pills scraped across the cracked glass of borrowed smartphones. The nights were always too large for our ribs, so we tore ourselves open to let them in, welcoming that sharp, chemical copper at the back of our throats, laughing until our lungs tasted like soot and sunrise. 

We treated our youth like stolen cars—revving the engine until the oil burned black and the tires screamed against the asphalt. Do you remember Marcus, his pupils swollen into total eclipses, tracing constellations in the bleach stains of a dive bar bathroom floor? He swore he could hear the color of the bass through the wood, swore we were all going to live forever as long as the music didn't stop. Now his name is just a quiet weight carried in the pockets of those who survived, whispered over paper cups of bitter coffee in rooms where nobody dances anymore. We spilled our tomorrows out onto kitchen counters, chopping them into fine, straight lines with expired IDs, desperately trying to snort away the morning because the daylight felt like an indictment of the chaos we loved.

How brilliant we were, bleeding out our innocence in gas station parking lots, convinced that to burn fast was the only way to prove we were on fire at all. The ghosts stay in the marrow now. I see Sarah in every flickering neon sign—Sarah, who chased a synthetic sun so far past the horizon she simply forgot how to return. The rest of us stumbled into the cold geography of our thirties, bruised and quieted, carrying the silence of the ones who stayed behind in the dark. We traded our hearts for the rush and our lungs for the smoke, left now with only this aching, beautiful rust, still loving them—those ruined, luminous meteors—for the magnificent wreck we made of the night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic literary vignette in the style of Denis Johnson about growing up taking wild risks—like doing whippets in a dugout or skitchin' behind cars—and reflecting on addiction and survival.
counterfactuals.output:
The snow on 4th Street wasn’t snow so much as grey slush, thick as lard and smelling of old coal. We were sixteen, made of wet wool, bad teeth, and a terrible, violent lightness. 

When Miller’s old man’s station wagon slowed down at the blinking yellow light, Jimmy and I dropped onto our knees in the street, our gloved hands snapping onto the chrome bumper like iron traps. That was skitchin’. The world went sideways at thirty miles an hour, your sneakers screaming over the ice, the hot blue exhaust blowing straight into your teeth. You held on because if your grip slipped, your skull hit the curb and you were just another piece of meat the plow would push into the gutter come daylight. We laughed until our lungs felt full of broken glass. We thought we were terrifying the adults. We didn’t know the adults were already dead inside, and we were just sprinting toward the edge of the same dark hole.

Later, when the sun died completely—that sickly, orange-gray twilight that only exists over flat Midwest towns—we’d crawl into the visitor’s dugout at the Little League park. 

It was cold enough to freeze the spit in your mouth. We sat on the splintered green bench with a box of silver chargers we’d lifted from the back of the kitchen where Jimmy washed dishes. The little brass cracker was cold as a gun barrel. You’d screw it down—*hiss*—and the balloon would bloom in the dark like a rubber lung.

You inhaled, and the universe instantly turned into a helicopter blade. *Wub-wub-wub-wub.* 

For thirty seconds, you weren't a high school drop-out living in a house that smelled like stale beer and boiling cabbage. You were an angel suspended in the high, cold rafters of heaven, looking down at your own cheap sneakers resting in the mud. The sky opened up and showed you its glowing gears, and God stood there, grinning like a butcher, holding a handful of sparklers. Then the gas wore off, the helicopter crashed into the dirt, and you were just a shivering kid with a headache, a metallic taste in his mouth, and a desperate, clawing need to do it again.

It was cheap back then. It was just gravity and compressed air and bad luck. We thought we were playing games with the sky.

We didn't know the game was real, or that it had already started keeping score. 

Jimmy went first, though he didn't die right away. He just traded the bumper of the station wagon for a brown paper bag full of paint cans, and then the cans for a belt and a spoon in a room above a laundromat in Spokane. The last time I saw him, his eyes looked like two burnt holes in a mattress. 

I don't know why I got out. I don't have a story about finding Jesus or checking into a clinic with white curtains. I just woke up one morning on a porch in Portland, smelling of my own old sweat and wet dog, with a heart that felt like a bird trapped in a cardboard box, and realized I hadn't died yet. 

Now I sit in this kitchen. The coffee is hot and black and plain. My hands don't shake much anymore, but sometimes, when an old car backfires down on the avenue, or when the air gets that specific, biting smell of late November frost, my knees ache with the ghost of that frozen slush. 

I think about us in that dugout, thirty years ago, silver metal cartridges littering the mud like spent shell casings. We were so eager to leave our bodies, so sure we could jump out of our skins and come back whenever we wanted. 

Some of us couldn't find the way back in. And those of us who did—well, we inhabit these old bones like squatters in a house the city's marked for demolition, just sitting by the window, watching the streetlights come on, wondering who gave us permission to stay.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about trying to quiet an inner ache when you were young. Use vivid, sensory imagery of cold weather, nitrous canisters, heroin, and broken bones.
counterfactuals.output:
The frost came early that year, biting deep
into the marrow of the late November air.
Breath bloomed white in the alleyway,
a brief ghost rising from cold, chapped lips,
then vanishing into the iron dark.

We sought a stillness in the freeze,
anything to blunt the quiet thrumming in the chest—
that hollow, hungry ache that grew 
whenever the sun dropped below the treeline.

In the snow, the small silver cylinders lay scattered,
spent nitrous canisters glinting like fallen shell casings.
A sharp, sweet rush of cold inside the lungs,
a metallic rattle behind the teeth,
the world warping into a high, thin pitch
until the pavement stopped swaying, if only for a second.

And when that wasn't heavy enough to drown the noise,
there was the darker shadow:
the bitter dust, the slow, thick velvet 
that pulled the cold right out of the room.
A false warmth spreading through the veins,
heavy as lead, soft as ash,
erasing the edges of the room,
erasing the memory of skin and stone.

Underneath it all, the old injuries hummed.
A collarbone once snapped like a dry winter twig,
ribs that had knitted back crooked in the dark.
In the damp cold, those broken bones remembered 
every impact, every sudden stop,
throbbing like a muffled bell beneath the coat.

We were so young, trying to freeze a fire,
trying to mend a fracture with a shadow,
paying for a moment's hush
with everything we had left to burn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a single long-sentence prose poem that uses repeated "Like..." clauses to recall dangerous childhood memories, ending with a reflection on seeing neighborhood kids years later.
counterfactuals.output: Like the summer we leapt from the high wooden trestle into the swollen black river without knowing what rocks lay beneath the froth, like the copper taste of terror when the five-o'clock freight train roared past, shaking the rusty bolts just inches from our bare toes, like steering our brakeless bicycles down the loose gravel of Dead Man’s Hill with our eyes squeezed tight against the stinging dust, like crouching in the toxic shadow of the abandoned chemical plant where the floorboards groaned beneath our thumping hearts, and like testing the gray ice at the quarry’s edge until it cracked beneath our boots with the sharp report of a rifle, I stand today at the window watching the new children of this street glide down the pristine sidewalk on their pastel scooters with bright helmets strapped snug beneath their unscarred chins, their easy laughter floating up through the warm air, and I catch my breath at the fragile, miraculous line between their protected present and the wild, dangerous ghosts we so narrowly survived becoming.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short creative piece about the desperate, quiet reasons teenagers turn to drugs and danger, and the grief of watching your old friend group disperse to death and prison.
counterfactuals.output:
Nobody outside the circle ever understood that it wasn’t about the rebellion. It wasn’t about being cool, or bad, or brave. 

It was about the noise. 

By fifteen, the world inside our heads had become a deafening, metallic scree—the hum of broken homes, the crushing gray weight of a town that felt like a trap, the quiet terror of looking into the future and seeing absolutely nothing at all. We didn’t take those pills or smoke that chemical fire because we wanted to see god. We took them because we wanted the static to stop. We just wanted a blanket made of smoke to throw over the cold, sharp edges of being alive.

Danger was the only thing that felt real. When Leo drove his dad’s rusted Civic ninety miles an hour down County Route 4 with the headlights off, we weren’t trying to die. We were begging the darkness to give us a reason to hold our breath, to force our hearts to hammer against our ribs so hard that, for ten seconds, we knew for a fact we were still here.

We were a pack of six. A tight, bruised little constellation sitting on the warm hood of a car behind the abandoned strip mall, passing cheap liquor and foil packets like sacred rites. We promised we’d get out. We promised we were different.

Then the quiet reasons started collecting their interest.

Maya was the first to slip out of the frame. Her quiet reason was a father who left and a mother who drank, leaving her with an emptiness so heavy she tried to fill it with white powder until her heart simply gave up on a Tuesday morning. She was seventeen. At her funeral, her parents sat on opposite sides of the aisle, refusing to look at each other, while the rest of us stood in the back, trembling in our oversized suits, smelling of stolen perfume and fresh panic.

Next was Leo. Leo, whose quiet reason was a terror of being invisible so deep it made him burn. He started with small thefts, moved to breaking down doors, chasing a high that wasn't in a bottle anymore, but in the kick of an adrenaline-soaked bolt-cutter. Last year, a judge gave him twelve years. Now, his life is measured in collect calls, plastic chairs, and glass walls. When I visit him, his laugh sounds hollowed out, like an echo trapped in a drainpipe.

One by one, the constellation burned down. 

Toby is buried three plots down from Maya, a victim of a bad batch on a hot July night. Sam is in state farm, serving a mandatory minimum that will eat the rest of his twenties. 

And then there’s me. Left behind in the quiet. 

I sit on the edge of the old concrete culvert where we used to hide, listening to the crickets. The grief doesn't scream; it sits on my chest like a lead weight. It’s a strange, ghost-filled kind of mourning. I am grieving the dead, yes, but I am also grieving the living who are locked in concrete boxes, and the kids we were before the desperate, quiet things in our hearts grew teeth and tore us apart.

I pull my jacket tight against the evening chill. The world is quiet now, just like we always wanted. But it is a graveyard quiet, and I would give anything to hear the noise again, if only it brought them back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
